title: Election date? Brexit reset outcome? Farage’s survival chances? Andrew Sparrow answers your questions
description:
The Guardian’s UK politics blogger is conducting a live Q&A

These are from my colleague Peter Walker, who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor.

Peter posted this before the result was announced.

Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again

Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number

Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport
text: Final questions, on far-right in Europe, Boris Johnson, Reform UK in the Senedd, the EU-UK reset deal, and Guardian comments
Before I wrap up, I will try some quickfire responses.

double quotation markI have a question Andrew: Do you think that our leaving the EU has enabled the far right parties in Europe to gain a bigger stronghold than if we had remained. I personally feel that we were something of a stabilising influence despite our moaning on about everything. I would be interested in what you and your colleagues think.

I don’t think Brexit had an impact on the rise of far-right parties in the EU countries – other than to discourage some of them, which had been toying with the idea of backing withdrawal from the EU, to give up on the idea because it ended so badly for the UK.
But it did shift the balance of power in the European Council a bit away from the northern, fiscal discipline bloc.
double quotation markDear Andrew, is it true Boris is going to make a comeback?

I don’t think that is likely any time soon. There is no opening for him either in the Conservative party, or in Reform UK. But he is only in his early 60s. It is not impossible that, at some point in the next 10 years, some cause crops up that he can make his own, and voters give him another chance because they have forgotten about partygate.
Mousebirdbadger asks:

double quotation markHello again. My question - if the official opposition (Reform) is boycotting the Senedd/ Welsh assembly and going to the pub instead, can they as individual MSs be recalled for dereliction of duty, or some such charge?
I don’t know enough about the Senedd rules to give you an answer on this. I did ask a colleague who covers Wales, who told me: “Possibly? But it hasn’t been mooted so far - it’s all untested waters.”

But to take action against the entire Reform UK group in the Senedd would look like victimising the party, and would send a terrible signal to the 29% of Welsh voters who supported them in the elections.
double quotation markQuestion for Andrew: Will Andy Burnham’s new EU deal improve or worsen Labour’s polling ratings and therefore their electoral chances?
Andy Burnham thinks it will be popular, and polling seems to confirm this.
double quotation markHow are you bearing up with the absence of a daily comments thread, Andrew? Did your plea for readers to get in touch / engage via other channels have much effect?
I miss the comments. Some people get in touch using the politics.live@theguardian.com email, but not many. It would be nice to get more. You can also find me on Bluesky.
Q&A: Can politicians still deliver great speeches?

double quotation markHi Andrew - nice to have you back. Or us back, I guess. Thanks for the blog. As someone who must follow the daily political shenanigans more than most, do you find the way it functions depressing? Less the positions or the policies, but the mechanisms of it - in particular the regular pretence that anybody from another party is absolutely wrong; that anything you disagree with is a laughable disgrace; that politicians who know very well how difficult the problems are pretend it’s just government incompetence that means they aren’t solved; and the general poverty of discourse. I’ve been re-reading some of the speeches from around the abolition of slavery, and I just can’t imagine any modern politician reaching the same level of rhetoric, or of nuance, now. Even 20 years ago, I remember some politicians who gave cracking speeches in parliament, raising really interesting perspectives. Tony Benn was a great speaker, but I always liked Tony Wright too. Do MPs still give interesting speeches, and I just don’t see them? Or is it just me growing grumpy grumpier with age, and harking back to some prelapsarian idyll that never really existed? If not, and you think there is an issue with the *how* of modern politics, do you see any particular causes, or any possible solutions? To me, we seem to have more public debate than ever, and nearly all of it seems almost entirely banal and pointless.

Until now, I have been choosing questions where I felt reasonably well qualified to give an answer. I posted this one because it is interesting and challenging; I’m not sure I do have an answer, but here goes anyway.

Years ago I wrote a book that involved reading 19th century debates and, I agree, they require a level of concentration that would be beyond most parliamentarians, or listeners, now. But that parliamentary debate was an elite activity, it was a pre-democratic age, and there was no TV.

Even 30 years ago, the speech was a key communication device in British politics. People like Gordon Brown regarded a good speech as the way you shifted public opinion. I don’t think there are many political leaders who think quite like that now; they still deliver speeches, but soundbites, interviews, social media clips, tweets and TikToks are often their preferred ways of getting the message across.
(There are exceptions; Alan Milburn grew up in the ‘speeches matter’ school of politics, and the speech he gave launching his report this week was powerful stuff.)

That does not mean today’s politicians are less intelligent; I think it’s about attention spans being shorter, and people being exposed to multiple sources of information at the same time. Wilberforce would have been rubbish on Twitter.

Does it mean public debate is more banal and pointless? I fear it does, though Substack and podcasts show that there are still plenty of people in politics who know how to articulate an argument at length.
Q&A: What is happening on PR and Lords reform?
Here are two questions on constitutional reform.

double quotation markAS - what is the mood music in the halls of govt about PR? Does PLP/Gov really want to change our political voting system and does it need to be a referendum or could it go into a manifesto but with added risk?

double quotation markQuestion Andrew: What is happening with the Labour manifesto commitment to hold public consultation on proposals to replace the House of Lords with an alternative second chamber more representative of the UK’s nations and regions?
At the moment, almost nothing is happening on electoral reform or Lords reform.

In his Labour conference speech, Andy Burnham said he would set up a national commission on electoral reform. He is probably more committed to PR than any previous Labour PM, even Tony Blair. But, since conference, we have heard zilch about this.

My understanding is that No 10 was determined to show it was focused on the cost of living in the first 100 days, and opening a debate on PR was viewed as a distraction. With Europe, social care reform, and the Milburn report also taking up a lot of time, Burnham may feel he does not have the bandwidth for this. As Rob Ford explained on Bluesky recently, the Green party’s “Zionism is racism” motion did not help the PR cause in Labour circles either.
On Lords reform, there is also radio silence.

But they might be connected. In his conference speech, Burnham did not commit to including PR in the Labour manifesto. He said they would fight the next election “with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard”. I don’t know what he had in mind when he drafted those words, but you could propose some form of elected element for the Lords which would be consistent with making sure “everyone’s voice is heard” but which would not be PR for the Commons. At a pinch, I suppose you could argue the supplementary vote for mayoral elections would meet this pledge, provided enough people had a mayor to vote for.
Q&A: How can Burnham justify wanting a rerun of the Brexit referendum, but not allowing a rerun of the Scottish independence one?

double quotation markAndrew: How can Burnham say “no discussion on constitutional issues” in relation to Scotland yet take entirely the opposite view wrt the EU? At what point will the media notice the hypocrisy?

We have noticed, and you are right to say these two positions are inconsistent. But there is an important difference. Andy Burnham wants to overturn the 2016 Brexit vote; he doesn’t want to overturn the 2014 IndyRef.
It is not unreasonable for a PM to refuse to do something if he regards it as a bad idea.

At some point, that position would be impossible to sustain if the Scottish people made it clear that they did want independence. We may get to that point in the end. But, with the independence polling still roughly in 50/50 territory, I think Burnham will be able to hold off on granting a referendum for some time.
Q&A: Why did Burnham keep Shabana Mahmood as home secretary?

double quotation markAndrew: why do you think Burnham kept Mahmood as Home Secretary and what are his options for getting rid of her now, given that she seems to have her own agenda which is inimical to the progressive alliance Burnham appears to want?

We think that Andy Burnham was minded to make Shabana Mahmood chancellor at one point and then lost his nerve – perhaps because he thought she would be too independent-minded, and because he thought John Healey would be more amenable.

You might be assuming that Andy Burnham is more liberal than he actually is. Remember, one of his chief mentors in politics was David Blunkett. His career flourished under Tony Blair. And this is what Burnham told Pippa Crerar in an interview during the Makerfield byelection campaign, when she asked about Reform UK claims he was pro-immigration. He said:

double quotation markI’m not like that. You know me. I was in the Home Office under Tony Blair, and actually, it was my job to return people. That was my specific role. I used to have to travel to governments around the world and persuade them to take back planes of people who had come here with no basis to stay, so you know, I never have been shy of getting to grips with these difficult issues.

Burnham forced Mahmood to water down her indefinite leave to remain plans. But I don’t think he wants an ultra-liberal home secretary, having her there has not so far stopped him winning back Green and Lib Dem voters, and I assume he thinks she is doing a decent job reducing the salience of immigration as an issue.
Q&A: Has James Cleverly got any chance of being elected London mayor?
double quotation markAndrew, has James Cleverly got any hope in becoming London’s mayor? At the moment it’s a toss up between none and Bob I think.

According to these odds, James Cleverly is at 6/1 – with Sadiq Khan the firm favourite. That looks about right. (They also have Laila Cunningham, the Reform UK candidate, at 3/1, which seems to rate her chances of winning far too high.) Cleverly may look like a no hope candidate now but, as Peter Walker pointed out earlier (see 10.58am), he is a much stronger candidate than any of the last three Tories to stand. Khan has never been an outstanding campaigner and, if he does not run again, the Labour figures being talked about as potential alternatives don’t sound impressive either. And Cleverly has a year and a half to carve out a distinct, liberal, London-friendly version of Conservatism that could work in 2028. It would mean distancing himself from Kemi Badenoch and the national party. But Tory high command would allow that, as they did with Boris Johnson when he won in 2008.
Q&A: Why is Badenoch getting more popular, and will she still be Tory leader at next election?
Here are two questions about Kemi Badenoch.

double quotation markQuestion for Andrew: I look at Badenoch and I listen to her interviews and I find her spectacularly abrasive and underprepared to answer detailed questions. That’s obviously a value-judgement on my part, but on major policy issues such as the UK involvement in the Iran War, Israel/Gaza, US-UK relations in the context of Madelson and Chagos she seems to make the opportunistic-but-wrong call. That said, her approval ratings are growing and people seem to really like her. I’d be interested to hear your reflections on what you think people are responding to so positively about her policies and her approach. Is it simply that it makes a good insta clip?
double quotation markAndrew, do you think Kemi Badenoch will last till the election as leader of the opposition? And dare I ask, who are the possible replacements.
Kemi Badenoch’s approval ratings are going up. But that is not because she is getting more popular with people like oidptg1 (ie, Guardian reading types).

Peter Kellner, the former YouGov president, wrote a good article on his Substack blog over the summer explaining what is going on. He says her ratings have shot up because she has won over voters on the right. Here is an excerpt.

double quotation markLast October, Conservative voters were even more likely than the wider public to say Badenoch did NOT look like a prime minister in waiting. Her figures are now very different. The percentage of Tory voters who say she DOES look like a PM in waiting has jumped from 17 to 62, while the percentage who disagree has slumped from 67 to 25. In half a century of monitoring poll findings, I cannot recall a leader’s appeal to their own party’s voters rising so dramatically. Badenoch has transformed her credibility among those who voted Tory in 2024 but were disillusioned by her performance in her first year as party leader. She has won the first round in her battle to revive her party’s fortunes and see off Farage.
And here are two charts illustrating this point.
Badenoch is “spectacularly abrasive”. But she is abrasive towards leftwingers, and so right-leaning voters seem to like that.

As to whether she will stay until the next election, yes, almost certainly. There is no desire at all in the party (MPs, peers, members, donors or the Tory press) to get rid of her. There are no rivals trying to get rid of her. And it is not even obvious that anyone else could do a better job, given that the policy decisions that might make the Tories more electable are unacceptable to the party at large.
Q&A: What will happen with the Farage inquiry, and will he stay on as Reform UK leader?
And here are two questions about Nigel Farage.

double quotation markAndrew - given Nigel’s net favourability is under water and RefUK Ltd continue to slide in the polls, do you think Nigel has had enough and might step aside, and if so how do you think the future plays out for them?

double quotation markHi Andrew, What’s the latest on the Farage donations scandal? It appears to be dragging on. And do you think Farage will fight on if found guilty and recalled? I note Farage is on record stating he expects an adverse result citing the usual “Establishment Plot” nonsense.

Reform UK has had a bad year but – unless there is something serious happening in his private life, or with his health, that we don’t know about – I find it very, very, very hard to imagine Nigel Farage stepping away before the election. This is a guy who devoted himself to a cause (leaving the EU) that for at least 15 years was a complete no-hope enterprise. He likes campaigning, he is good at it, and he still has an outside chance of being PM. Why would he give it up?

Re the donations scandal, we think the parliamentary commissioner for standards has written his report and it is now with the standards committee. They can spend months dealing with these matters. I would be amazed if the commissioner has not concluded that Farage broke the rules by not declaring the £5m Harborne donations; the rules are clear that, if there could be a perception of a donation being linked to parliamentary activity, it should be declared. But I think it is possible the committee could find a way of not recommending a long suspension. That would be quite a perverse finding; but its conclusions in the James McMurdock case were almost unbelievably lenient.
If they do recommend a suspension of 10 days or more, I think there will be a recall byelection, and Farage will win again, quite easily.
Q&A: Where is Andy Burnham's desire for a closer relationship with the EU going to end up?
Here are two related questions on Andy Burnham’s desire for a closer relationship with the EU.

double quotation markWRT the article and topic of the EU indicating it won’t discuss long term permanent close relations until it is assured Burnham is serious, do you think this will mean Burnham is treading water on this subject until after a GE has been fought with the specific issue of a much closer relationship with the EU in (or out) of party manifestos in the UK?
And DownsideUp asks:

double quotation markHi Andrew. Do you think that the pro-EU campaign is being complacent in not having a co-ordinated campaign in place? It seems that the “Stay Out” campaign group is setting the terms of the debate. For example, I already know that slogan but I don’t even know if their opponents are Remainers/Rejoiners/Joiners. I have even less idea what a new EU relationship would look like. It feels a reset has been launched on a whim.

I think there is going to be a lot of treading water on this for some time. I don’t think anyone can predict the outcome of this process with any confidence at all until we know the results of the next election.

Andy Burnham is on record as saying that he would like to rejoin, and I think he is sincere in wanting to achieve a radical shift. But he has also – right from the moment he opened this debate in his conference speech – stressed his desire to find a consensus. I think there will come a point, at some point in the future, when there is a strong consensus (say, 70/30) in favour of rejoining. But I think that could take a decade, at least, and it would probably require the Tories to have a leader willing to disown the Brexit cult and say it has been a mistake. Before that, there might be a firm consensus sooner behind some sort of Swiss option.

Re the second question, it would be hard for the pro-EU side to have a campaign in place when they don’t know where they are heading. But I think No 10 have been a bit alarmed about quite how quickly and forcefully the Stay Out campaign has launched. Stay Out are trying to shape the terms of the debate. Years ago Dominic Cummings led a campaign against joining the euro. Tony Blair never opted for this in the end and Cummings argued afterwards (rightly) that just ensuring the referendum never happened in the first place was a strategic victory for his side.

Burnham gets criticised for launching this debate without seeming to know where he wants it to end up. Personally, I don’t think that’s necessarily a bad thing. He’s testing public opinion, and seeing where it will go. We may be surprised. I’ve been struck by how, even though Stay Out have marshalled some strong arguments against rejoining, no one is seriously contesting Burnham’s claim that Brexit has done more harm than good. Stay Out are making other arguments. On the key point of contention, Burnham seems to have won already.
From now on, I will be focusing on the Q&A.
To follow what is happening at the Coalition of the Willing summit, do read Jakub Krupa’s Europe live blog.
Q&A: When will the next election happen?

double quotation mark@Andrew - gov must call a GE by August 2029. Burnham has ruled out a 2027 GE, so do you think that means we’ll have one in 2028? Because it’s inconceivable they’d wait till 2029 when gov has to cut spending isn’t it?

The conventional wisdom in British politics is that prime ministers call elections on the first Thursday after they have been in office for four years and when polling suggests they will win. Often this ends up as the first Thursday in May, when local elections happen anyway.

That is because a PM with a decent chance of winning at that point normally does not want to risk ‘events’ taking away his or her lead, and leaving no room for manoeuvre, as the five-year hard deadline looms.
On that basis, 2028 would be a reasonable guess.

You are right to say Burnham has ruled out an election in 2027. Theresa May also ruled out an election in 2017 – until she changed her mind. It is not impossible that Burnham might do this. But voters don’t like early elections, and dozens of Labour MPs would probably lose their seats, and so I can only see that happening unless Burnham can come up with a very, very good pretext to justify one. I think that’s unlikely. (And I hope it won’t happen too – I’ve booked a holiday for next spring.)

As Jennifer Rankin reports, one of the issues still being haggled over at the last minute ahead of tomorrow’s UK-EU reset deal has been how many young EU nationals would be allowed to come to Britain under the youth mobility scheme.
In a report for the i, Arj Singh says the EU seems to have won this one. He says:

double quotation markThe UK and EU have provisionally agreed there will be a cap of 100,000 visas on a landmark Brexit reset deal to allow easier travel, work and study for under-32s between the two areas, The i Paper has learnt … It means 100,000 Brits stand to benefit from easier arrangements to travel, work and study in the EU from as early as 2028, with a final deadline of 2030, and vice versa. The i Paper has also learnt the UK and EU have agreed the scheme will be open to those aged 18 to 31 on the first day of their intended stay on the other side, despite initial suggestions it would only be open to under-30s.
Singh says this still needs to be signed off by EU member states. He adds:

double quotation markThe final 100,000 represents a late compromise from the UK, which had been pushing for 80,000, but British negotiators are likely to regard it as a fair one given the EU’s initial push for an uncapped scheme.
